reason: The narrative of Judges 9 explicitly undermines any notion of elite superiority. Abimelech, the would-be elite ruler, commits fratricide against his 70 brothers and establishes his rule through violence and mercenary support. The parable of the trees illustrates that those unfit for leadership (the thornbush) eagerly accept power, while the truly useful are reluctant. The text demonstrates that both the 'elite' (Abimelech) and the people (Shechem) make destructive choices and suffer equal divine judgment. The narrative arc shows mutual betrayal, warfare, and destruction affecting all parties, suggesting that neither elite nor common people are inherently better, but rather both are subject to moral accountability and divine justice. The text functions as a cautionary tale against such hierarchical assumptions.
